newsitem.title: USA: Florida sues U.S. government over immigration.
newsitem.headline: Florida sues U.S. government over immigration.

text.p: Florida sued the U.S. government on Wednesday, saying federal welfare changes will cost the state $1 billion a year in services to legal immigrants whose federal benefits end on Aug. 1.

Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles said the state does not have the money to pick up the tab for an estimated 100,000 legal immigrants in Florida affected by the federal cuts that Congress approved last year. He said the 1996 Welfare Reform Act illegally denies disabled and elderly legal immigrants access to supplemental Security Income and food stamps.
The state is asking that benefits be restored to legal non-citizens and that the cuts be declared null and void.

"We're talking about people who followed the rules," Chiles told a Tallahassee news conference. "They came here legally, came with a green light from our government. We welcomed them and many have worked very hard. Now, the federal government is rewarding them with a push and a shove."
Dade County, which encompasses the Miami urban area, joined the state as a plaintiff. An estimated 50,000 Dade residents face cuts that Metro-Dade Mayor Alex Penelas said would be devastating.
"There people are legal residents," Penelas said. "Many of them have worked hard, paid taxes and they have contributed significantly to their communities."

Three years ago, Florida sued the federal government to recoup state funds spent on services to illegal immigrants. In rejecting that suit, the courts said immigration policy was a political decision that could not be made by judges.

Though many legal immigrants have applied for citizenship and expect to receive it prior to the Aug. 1 cutoff, many others do not have the documentation necessary to apply, state officials said. Others have not lived in the United States long enough to be eligible.

Eduardo Marsans, a 21-year-old quadriplegic who immigrated legally to the United States in 1993, appeared with Chiles at the news conference. He receives SSI and food stamps but will lose the benefits because he has not been in the United States for the five years required to seek citizenship.

"I am grateful for the support the federal government has given us," Marsans' mother, Carmen Fernandez, said through an interpreter. "I have a question. What is going to happen to my son when he is denied his benefits? We came to this country legally and now they are treating us like the don't want us any more."
